greek_sentence: ἔτι δὲ ἀνεμεσητότερον οἶμαι τοῖς δυναμένοις ἀπολύσασθαι τὰ κακῶς εἰρημένα πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐγκλήματα, καθάπερ ἐν δικα στηρίῳ τοῖς ἀναγνωσομένοις ἀμφοτέρων τὰ γράμματα, τὴν ἀπολογίαν ποιήσασθαι, καὶ μάλιστα ὅταν ὁ μὲν ἐγκαλῶν πρὶν μαθεῖν τὰ λεγόμενα θρασύνεται, τῷ δ’ ἀπολογουμένῳ πεπαιδεῦσθαι κατὰ τοῦ παλαιοῦ δόγματος.
english_sentence_A: And it is, I think, still less a cause for reproach for those who are able to refute the charges ill brought against him to make their defence, as it were in a court of law, before those who will read the writings of both parties—and especially when the accuser grows bold before he has learned what is being said, while it falls to the one making the defence to have been educated in accordance with the ancient doctrine.
english_sentence_B: And it is, I think, still less a cause for indignation that those who are able to refute the charges wrongly brought against him should make their defence, as in a law-court, before those who will read the writings of both parties; and especially when the accuser grows bold before he has learned what is being said, while the defender has been educated in the ancient doctrine.

greek_sentence: τά τε γὰρ ἐπαινούμενα Λύκου φαντάσματά ἐστιν, οὐχὶ Ἱπποκράτους δόγματα, δι’ ὧν τε ἀντιλέγει δῆλός ἐστι μηδὲ τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς Ἱπποκράτους τέχνης ἐπιστάμενος.
english_sentence_A: For the things he praises are phantasms of Lycus, not doctrines of Hippocrates, and in the things by which he contradicts him he is manifestly ignorant even of the elements of the Hippocratic art.
english_sentence_B: For the things he praises are Lycus' own fancies, not the doctrines of Hippocrates, and by the arguments with which he contradicts him he is plainly not acquainted even with the elements of the Hippocratic art.

greek_sentence: οὔτε γὰρ ὅσοι δόγμασιν ἐναντίοις ἐνεγράφησαν οὔθ’ ὅσοι μήτε τὰ πρῶτα γινώσκουσι τῆς τέχνης χρήσιμα εὔλογον ἐξηγεῖσθαι τοὺς ἀφορισμοὺς, ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ μεμαθήκασι μὲν ἐκ τῆς παιδικῆς ἡλικίας, ἐπαινοῦσι δὲ πάλιν ἢ ψέγουσιν αὐτοῦ τὰ δόγματα.
english_sentence_A: For it is not reasonable that either those who have been enrolled under opposing doctrines, or those who do not even know the first useful things of the art, should expound the Aphorisms; but, as though they had learned them from childhood, they praise or again censure his doctrines.
english_sentence_B: For it is not reasonable that either those who have enrolled themselves under contrary doctrines, or those who do not know even the first useful things of the art, should expound the Aphorisms; but rather, just as they have learned them from the age of childhood, so they in turn praise or censure his doctrines.

english_sentence_A: The patients sweat from the first day, yet are benefited by these sweats either moderately or not at all: these fevers I call wet; and conversely I call dry those fevers in which there is violent thirst, a dry tongue, skin hard like a hide, and much parching dryness throughout the whole body.

english_sentence_B: Just as, then, in water and stone and air a commensurate heat arises, so also in the case of vapour: when, being well-mixed, it fills the bath, the bathers are annoyed and find fault with such a bath, yet they do not call it colder or hotter; so that if it also does something of that kind, they make a double charge against the bath, declaring it to be cold and full of vapour, just as also, again, hot beyond measure with abundant vapour.

greek_sentence: μὴ τοίνυν ἐπιλανθανώμεθα τούτων μηδὲ τὰ κοινῇ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις γιγνωσκόμενα διαφθείρωμεν ὑπὸ περιττῆς σοφίας, ἣν ἐπιδείκνυνταί τινες, ἀλλὰ μεμνημένοι τῶν βαλανείων, ἐπειδὰν ἀκούσωμέν τινος ἐπὶ ζώου λέγοντος, ὡς ἔστι τούτου μὲν εὔκρατον τὸ θερμὸν, τούτου δὲ δύσκρατον, [203] οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄλλο τι μεταφέρωμεν τὴν διάνοιαν, ἀλλ’ ἐφ’ ὅπερ ἅπαντες οἱ τὰς κοινὰς ἐννοίας διασώζοντες ἄνθρωποι, καθ’ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἐν ἄλλοις τε πολλοῖς καὶ μέντοι γε καὶ τοῖς βαλανείοις ὧν ἐμνημόνευσα.
english_sentence_A: Let us not, then, forget these things, nor corrupt what is known in common to all men through the superfluous wisdom which some people display; but, bearing the baths in mind, whenever we hear someone saying of an animal that the heat of this one is well-mixed, while that of this other is ill-mixed, [203] let us not transfer our thought to anything else, but to that very thing to which all men who preserve the common notions transfer it every day, in many other matters and indeed also in the baths which I have mentioned.

greek_sentence: ἐάσης οὖν ἤδη τὰ βαλανεῖα τῶν καθ’ ἑκάστην [204] ἡμέραν ἐν ταῖς οἰκίαις ἡμῖν συμβαινόντων ἀναμνήσθητί μοι, ποτὲ μὲν ὑγρότητα τῶν οἰκίων ἐν οἷς ἔσμεν, ἔστι δ’ ὅτε ἄμετρον ψύξιν ἢ θερμότητα μεμφόμεθα, πότερα μὲν οὖν ὁμοίως μεμφόμεθα τὸν κατὰ τὸν οἶκον ἀέρα τοῖς ὑπὸ κύνα καύμασι, κἀπειδὰν καπνοῦ πληρωθῇ, ἢ κἀνταῦθα ὥσπερ ἐν ταῖς βαλανείοις ἔστιν ὅτε κατὰ μὲν τὴν θερμασίαν διαλλάττουσιν οὐδὲν, ἔστι δ’ αὐτῶν ὁ μὲν αὐτὸ δὴ τοῦτο μόνον, ἀὴρ θερμὸς, ὁ δὲ σὺν τούτῳ καπνώδης, εἶτα ὁ μέν γε θερμὸς ἀὴρ οὐδέποτε προκαλεῖται δάκρυον, τῷ καπνώδει δ’ ἀεὶ ὑπάρχει τοῦτο κἂν μετρίως θερμὸς ᾖ, ὥστε ἐναργῶς ἐνταῦθα κατάδηλόν ἐστι τὸ δακνῶδες θερμὸν οὐ τῷ μᾶλλον θερμαίνειν, ἀλλ’ ἑτέρῳ τινὶ διαλλάττον.
english_sentence_A: Leaving the baths now, then, recall for me what happens to us every [204] day in our houses: sometimes we find fault with the dampness of the houses in which we are, at other times with immoderate cold or heat. Do we then find fault with the air in the house in the same way in the heats under the Dog-star as when it has been filled with smoke, or is it here too, as in the baths, that sometimes they differ not at all in heat, yet one of them is just this alone, hot air, while the other is, along with this, smoky; and then the hot air never provokes tears, whereas the smoky air always does this, even if it is only moderately hot; so that here it is evidently plain that the biting heat differs not by heating more, but by something else.

Do we then find fault with the air in the house in the same way in the heats under the Dog-star as when it has been filled with smoke, or is it here too, as in the baths, that sometimes they differ not at all in heat, yet one of them is just this alone, hot air, while the other is, along with this, smoky; and then the hot air never provokes tears, whereas the smoky air always does this, even if it is only moderately hot; so that here it is evidently plain that the biting heat differs not by heating more, but by something else.
english_sentence_B: Leave the baths now, then, and recall for me the things that happen to us every [204] day in our houses: sometimes we find fault with the dampness of the houses we are in, at other times with immoderate cold or heat. Do we then find fault in the same way with the air in the house during the burning heats under the Dog Star and when it has been filled with smoke?

greek_sentence: θαυμαστὸν οὖν εἴ τις ἐπὶ καπνοῦ καὶ φλογὸς αἰσθάνεται [205] τῆς διαφορᾶς, ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἡμετέρων σωμάτων ἀναίσθητός ἐστιν ἐνίοτε μὲν ἰσχυροτάτης θερμασίας οἷον φλογὸς, ἐνίοτε δὲ ἀνιαρᾶς καὶ δακνώδους οἷόν περ καπνοῦ.
english_sentence_A: It is astonishing, then, if someone perceives [205] the difference in the case of smoke and flame, but in the case of our bodies is insensible of a heat that is sometimes very strong, like that of flame, and sometimes distressing and biting, like that of smoke.
english_sentence_B: It is surprising, then, if someone perceives [205] the difference in the case of smoke and flame, yet in the case of our own bodies is insensible that the warmth is sometimes most intense, like that of flame, and sometimes distressing and biting, like that of smoke.

english_sentence_A: And I am no less astonished if he does not concede that the ill-mixtures in respect of heat in animals are analogous to those in baths and houses; as, then, in houses the air of a smoky house is one thing, and that of a simply hot house another, in the same way, I think, evidently different from these is that air in which there is a multitude of burning lamps or of torch-wood together with soot, and accordingly we also call this sooty, just as we call the other air smoky, since it arises from the over-roasting of material.

english_sentence_A: So too among plants one is a tree, another a shrub, another a thorn, another a herb, another brushwood; or, although all of them, in the respect in which they are conceived as animals, have no difference, would one not nonetheless truly call all these which he has mentioned, and not a few others besides these, differences of animal?

Or, although all things, insofar as they are conceived as animals, have no difference, may one nevertheless not truly call all these that have been mentioned, and besides these not a few others, differences of animal?

english_sentence_A: ‘And we are not yet wise by either of these, neither because we know its unlimited nor because we know its one; but that we know how many [210] they are and of what sort, this is what makes each of us lettered.’ Protarchus: ‘Most true.’ Socrates: ‘And indeed what happens to make a man musical, this is the same thing.’ Protarchus: ‘How so?’ Socrates: ‘Sound, I suppose, is one in itself as regards that art too.’ Protarchus: ‘How could it not be?’ Socrates: ‘And let us posit two, low and high, and as a third the equal-toned; or how?’ Protarchus: ‘So.’ Socrates: ‘But you would not yet be wise in music knowing these things alone, while not knowing them you would be, so to speak, worth nothing in these matters.’ Protarchus: ‘Certainly not.’ Socrates:

english_sentence_A: For when you have grasped these very things in this way, then you have become wise; and when, inquiring in this way, you have got hold of any other of the things that are, you have thus become intelligent about it.’ These things from Plato, then, would have sufficed for hearers possessed of intelligence as a demonstration of the constitution of all the arts.

english_sentence_A: For it is not possible to become skilled in an art, not even in regard to a single thing, without knowing their differences; but it is no worse that, just as Plato himself was not content with the summary argument alone but added examples for the sake of clarity, grammar and music, so we too should add one further example, the art of painting, whose underlying matter is colours.

english_sentence_A: And indeed, if this is true, while they themselves think that both statements cannot be true — the one asserting that white is contrary to black, and the same one asserting that white does not differ at all from black insofar as it is colour — they will not be speaking correctly.
english_sentence_B: Now the man who in Plato's writing converses with Socrates was perhaps pardonable in preventing Socrates from dividing pleasure from pleasure by a difference.

greek_sentence: οὐ γὰρ ἦν που βιβλίον οὐδὲν τοιοῦτο διδάσκων, ὡς ἐγχωρεῖ πολλὰ πολλοῖς ὄντα τῷ γένει ταὐτὰ διαφέρειν ὅμως εἰς τοσοῦτον, ὡς ἐναντιώτατον ἀλλήλοις ἰδέαν τε καὶ φύσιν ἔχειν.
english_sentence_A: Now the man who converses with Socrates in Plato’s writing was perhaps pardonable in preventing Socrates from dividing pleasure from pleasure by a difference; for there was not yet, I suppose, any book teaching such a thing, namely that it is possible for many things, while being the same as many others in genus, nevertheless to differ to such an extent as to have a form and nature most contrary to one another.
english_sentence_B: For there was then, I suppose, no book teaching any such thing, namely that it is possible for many things that are the same in genus as many others nevertheless to differ to such a degree as to have a form and nature most contrary to one another.

english_sentence_A: Now the man who converses with Socrates in Plato’s writing was perhaps pardonable in preventing Socrates from dividing pleasure from pleasure by a difference; for there was not yet, I suppose, any book teaching such a thing, namely that it is possible for many things, while being the same as many others in genus, nevertheless to differ to such an extent as to have a form and nature most contrary to one another.
english_sentence_B: For there was then, I suppose, no book teaching any such thing, namely that it is possible for many things that are the same in genus as many others nevertheless to differ to such a degree as to have a form and nature most contrary to one another.

english_sentence_A: But since the Philebus was written by Plato teaching the truth, if Lycus did not read the book at all, I admire Lycus for his education; if he read it but did not understand it, I marvel at his intelligence; and if he understood it but was not persuaded, I congratulate him on his judgement.
english_sentence_B: But since the Philebus was written by Plato teaching the truth, if Lycus did not read the book at all, I admire Lycus for his education; if, having read it, he did not understand it, I marvel at his intelligence; and if, having understood it, he was not persuaded, I congratulate him on his judgement.

english_sentence_A: In wines, at any rate, that by which excellence is marked off from badness is stypticity from sourness; for the styptic wines are of noble quality, whereas none is sour by nature, but if even a little of such a quality comes upon them, we at once suspect their change into vinegar.
english_sentence_B: In wines, at any rate, in which excellence is distinguished from defect, astringency is distinguished from sourness: for the astringent wines are noble, whereas none is sour by nature, but if even a little of such a quality comes upon them, we at once suspect their change into vinegar.

english_sentence_A: For some things are melted by it, and it makes others set, and it transforms very many things; and, to speak of our bodies in particular, it digests the food in the stomach and the intestines, and conveys the product of its working-up into the body, and alters it into body and attaches it to our bodies, in nutrition and in growth.

english_sentence_A: These things being so, and the things sought in comparing one heat against another being three, as I have said before, when Hippocrates says here that those who are growing have the most innate heat, [one of three things follows]: either he uses this expression in its proper sense and has stated a falsehood, or he has used the expression badly and has also stated something false, or, in order that he may seem to have said something true, [231] he must have used the expression not well.
english_sentence_B: This being so, and the things inquired into in comparing one heat with another being three, as I said before, when Hippocrates says here that growing things have the most innate heat, [he does] one of three things: either, using this word in its proper sense, he has said something false; or he has used the word badly and said something false; or else, in order that he may seem to have said something true, [231] it must be that he has not used the word well.

english_sentence_A: For if he says that heat is greatest in those who are growing in the sense of according to substance, as one might also say that the moisture of the amphora is greatest, not that of the double of it, he will seem to have used the expression correctly, but it is necessary that he has stated a great falsehood.
english_sentence_B: For if he says that the heat is most in growing bodies, for instance in respect of substance, as one might say that the liquid of the amphora is most, not that of the double of it, he will seem to have used the word correctly, but he must necessarily have said something very false.

english_sentence_A: In not using the [232] expression well he would seem to go wrong because he applied this expression, which is assigned to what is greater in substance, wishing to signify that the quality is more intensified in respect of warming.
english_sentence_B: And he would seem to have said something false, because the heat in growing bodies is not most intensified in quality, not as it should be, hotter in this age than in any other.

english_sentence_A: But he said that it is most intensified in those who are growing; and that this is in fact false, that the heat is most intensified in those who are growing, is easy for anyone to establish.
english_sentence_B: For no sign would be found present in the body of growing persons of a greatest intensification of heat in warmth.

english_sentence_A: For no sign existing in the body would be found in those who are growing of the heat being most intensified in respect of warming.
english_sentence_B: For what was said by him in the treatise On the Nature of Man, as evidence that heat is most in growing bodies, is altogether foolish.

greek_sentence: οὐ γὰρ ἂν πρὸς βίαν, φησὶ, καὶ παρὰ φύσιν ἀνεφέρετο ἡ τροφὴ πρὸς ἐναντίον τῷ αὐτῆς [233] τῆς βάρει ἐν τῷ αὔξεσθαι τὸ σῶμα, εἰ μή τι ἰσχυρὸν τὸ ἐπαναγκάζον ᾖ.

english_sentence_A: Just as, then, he says in this way that a small child has a larger brain than the largest elephant, attending not to the bulk of the body alone but adding to it the consideration according to proportion, so he ought to have done in the case of the hot body too, having considered what sort of thing among the bodies in us is innate, that is, primordial.
english_sentence_B: Just as, then, he says that so small a child has a larger brain than the largest elephant, not directing his attention to the bulk of the body alone, but adding to it the consideration according to proportion, so also in the case of the hot body he ought to have done, considering what sort of body among those within us is innate, that is, primordial.

greek_sentence: ἀδιάπλαστος γάρ τις σὰρξ μαλακὴ παραπλήσιος αἵματος θρόμβῳ διαδέχεται τὴν πρώτην τοῦ κυήματος ἰδέαν, ἐν αὐτῇ τινας ἔχουσαν, καθάπερ Ἱπποκράτης ὠνόμασεν, οἶον αἱμάλωπας ἐκ τῆς τοῦ σπέρματος οὐσίας, τῆς ἐν αὐτῇ λευκότητος ὑπαρχούσης, ὕστερον δ’ ἐκ πολλῆς τῆς ἀλλοιώσεως συνεχῶς γιγνομένης, ὀστοῦ τις ὑπογραφὴ καὶ χόνδρου καὶ συνδέσμου καὶ νεύρου καὶ ἀρτηρίας καὶ φλεβὸς ἀποτελεῖται, καθ’ ὃν ἤδη χρόνον μένον ἔτι τὸ ἔμφυτον θερμὸν σῶμα [237] τοῖς κυουμένοις ἐστὶν, ἀλλὰ πλεῖστον ἀεί τε καὶ μᾶλλόν ἐστιν ὅσον αὔξεται τὰ κυούμενα.
english_sentence_A: For a certain unformed soft flesh, resembling a clot of blood, takes over the first appearance of the embryo, having within it certain things, as Hippocrates named them, like blood-weals, from the substance of the seed, the whiteness in it being present; and later, from the great alteration that comes about continuously, a kind of outline of bone and cartilage and ligament and nerve and artery and vein is brought to completion, at which time the innate hot body [237] is still remaining in those that are being carried in the womb, but it is always greatest, and the more so, in proportion as the things carried in the womb grow.
english_sentence_B: For an unformed, soft flesh, like a clot of blood, succeeds the first form of the embryo, having in it certain things which Hippocrates named, as it were, bloody streaks, deriving from the substance of the semen, its whiteness still being present in it; and later, as much alteration continually takes place, an outline of bone and cartilage and ligament and nerve and artery and vein is completed, at which time the innate hot body still remains [237] in the fetuses, but is greatest always and the more so as the fetuses grow.

english_sentence_A: For in all things that exist there are two qualities most suited for dispersal, moisture and heat, and conversely two for permanence, dryness and coldness; so that it is no wonder if the bodies of children, on account of their moisture and heat, are easily transpired, while those of the old are not easily so, since they have a substance congealed by dryness and cooling. So that, my excellent Lycus, you bring charges concerning the very things for which you ought to have been censured.

greek_sentence: Λύκος δὲ, ὡς οἶμαι, καὶ τὴν τετραφάρμακον ὀνομαζομένην δύναμιν, ἐκ κηροῦ καὶ στέατος καὶ πίττης καὶ ῥητίνης, ἴσων ἁπάντων συντεθειμένων, οὐ φήσει πλείονα μὲν πίτταν ἔχειν, ἐὰν διπλασίαν τις ἐμβάλλῃ τῶν ἄλλων, ἀλλὰ κἀνταῦθα ἐπισκέψασθαι, πότερον πίθος ὅλος ἐστὶ μεστὸς τῆς τετραφαρμάκου δυνάμεως ἢ μικρόν τι λεκάριον, εἴτα τὸν πίθον ἐρεῖ πολὺ πλείονα τὴν πίτταν ἔχειν τοῦ λεκαρίου, κἂν ὁ μὲν ἐξ ἴσων ἦν τῶν τεττάρων, ἡ πίττα δὲ ὑπάρχει διπλασία τῶν ἅλλων ἐν τῷ λεκαρίῳ.

greek_sentence: εἴπερ οὖν ἅπαντα τὰ τοιαῦτα ἁμαρτήματα ﻿ [241] τῶν ἄλλων μὴ δυναμένων ἐστὶ διακρῖναι τὸ κατ’ ἀναλογίαν καὶ μίξιν πολὺ τοῦ κατὰ τὸ κοινὸν μέτρον ἁπλῶς οὕτω λεγομένου, οὐ κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ἐφ’ ὃν ὁ Λύκος ἐνεκάλεσεν Ἱπποκράτει· ἥ τε γὰρ οὐσία τοῦ ἐμφύτου θερμοῦ πλείστη τοῖς αὐξανομένοις ἐστὶν, ὡς πρὸς τὴν τῶν ἄλλων ἀναλογίαν, ἥ τε σὺν αὐτῇ ποιότης ὡσαύτως, ἐπειδήπερ ἀχώριστοι τῶν οὐσιῶν εἰσιν αἱ οἰκεῖαι ποιότητες, ὥσπερ γε τῷ καὶ αἱ δυνάμεις.

english_sentence_B: This same thing one might say of the bath too, when it has in it not only the well-tempered air, but has also taken on some smoke and steam.

english_sentence_A: For of these, sometimes the smoke can be more, sometimes the vapour, just as also the air of the bath-house that is in accordance with nature.

english_sentence_A: And why need one mention the others, when we have a manifest witness to the argument in the fevers themselves, which everyone says every day have become greater or less than one another, and at times that someone is feverish less or more, and that this man's fever is the same yesterday or today?
english_sentence_B: And why need one mention other things, when we have a clear testimony to the argument in fevers themselves, which everyone daily says have sometimes become greater or less than one another, and sometimes that a man is feverish less or more, this one compared with the same man yesterday or today?

greek_sentence: οὕτως οὖν ὑποκειμένου λέγεσθαι τοῦ κατὰ τὴν ποιότητα πλέονος οὐδὲν θαυμαστὸν, ἐν ᾧ βαλανείῳ πλείων ἐστὶν οὐσία καπνοῦ καὶ τὴν ποιότητα φάναι γεγονέναι πλείονα καὶ τὴν ἐνέργειαν, εἰ μὲν κυρίως ὀνομάζομεν ἰσχυράν τε καὶ σφοδροτέραν, εἰ δὲ καταχρώμενοι μείζονά τε καὶ πλείονα.
english_sentence_A: With it thus laid down that the 'more' in respect of quality is so spoken of, it is no wonder, in a bath-house in which the substance of smoke is greater, to say that the quality too has become more, and the activity: 'strong' and 'more intense', if we are naming properly; 'greater' and 'more', if by misuse.
english_sentence_B: Since, then, the 'more' according to quality is assumed to be said in this way, it is no wonder that, in a bath in which there is more substance of smoke, one says that both the quality and the activity have become more: if we name them properly, strong and more intense; if by catachresis, greater and more.

english_sentence_A: For the smoke will evidently bite the eyes to the degree that it increases also in substance; so that, since the qualities proper to the substances and the activities always increase together with the substances, one might truly say that in such a bath-house the smoke is greatest.
english_sentence_B: For the smoke will clearly bite the eyes in proportion as it increases in substance too; so that, since the proper qualities and the activities always increase together with the substances, one would truly say that in such a bath the smoke is greatest.

greek_sentence: ὑποκείσθω δὲ πάλιν, ὡς ἐλέγομεν, [244] ἀτμοῦ τε καὶ καπνοῦ κατὰ τὸ βαλανεῖον ὑπάρχειν, ἡ δ’ οἰκεία τοῦ ἀέρος οὐσία, πλείστη κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν οὖσά τε καὶ γιγνομένη τοῦ τοῖς ζώοις ἐμφύτου θερμοῦ λεχθήσεται γὰρ καὶ νῦν ἐν τῷ βαλανείῳ πλεῖστον εἶναι τὸ οἰκεῖον θερμόν.
english_sentence_A: But let it be supposed again, as we were saying, [244] that there is something of vapour and of smoke in the bath-house, while the substance proper to the air both is and becomes greatest in proportion, like that of the heat innate in animals; for it will be said now too that in the bath-house the proper heat is greatest.
english_sentence_B: Let it be supposed again, as we were saying, [244] that there is some steam and smoke in the bath, while the proper substance of the air is greatest in proportion, being and becoming the analogue of the innate heat in animals; for now too it will be said that the proper heat in the bath is greatest.

english_sentence_A: Does it, then, fall at all short of this, that the humours in the animal too, from whose exhalation comes the heat that strikes those who touch it from outside?
english_sentence_B: Is anything, then, lacking from this in the case of the humours in the animal too, from whose vaporizing comes the warmth that meets those who touch from outside?

greek_sentence: τούτου γὰρ ἀναμιμνήσκειν ἀεὶ δεῖ, καθάπερ ὑπὸ ληθάργου κατεχομένους, τοὺς τὰ τοιαῦτα ληροῦντας ὁποῖα Λύκος ἔγραψεν, ἥ τε συναυξανομένη ποιότης οὖσα χρηστὴ καὶ φίλιος, οὐκ ἀνιαρὰ καὶ δακνώδης τοῖς ἁπτομένοις, ἤ τ’ ἐνέργεια, καθ’ ἣν αἱ πέψεις οὐ κνισώδεις γίνονται οὐδ’ ὀξώδεις ὡς ἐπὶ φλέγματος.
english_sentence_A: In the case of children, then, the substance of the blood is greatest according to the proportion of the mixture (for of this one must always remind, as if they were held fast by lethargy, those who talk such nonsense as Lycus wrote), and so is the quality that increases together with it, being wholesome and friendly, not distressing and biting to those who touch, and the activity, according to which the digestions become neither nidorous nor acid, as in the case of phlegm.
english_sentence_B: For of this one must always remind, as though they were held fast by lethargy, those who babble such things as Lycus wrote; and the quality that increases with it is wholesome and friendly, not distressing and biting to those who touch, and so is the activity, according to which the digestions become neither nidorous nor acid, as in the case of phlegm.

english_sentence_B: For of this one must always remind, as though they were held fast by lethargy, those who babble such things as Lycus wrote; and the quality that increases with it is wholesome and friendly, not distressing and biting to those who touch, and so is the activity, according to which the digestions become neither nidorous nor acid, as in the case of phlegm.

english_sentence_A: For you have shown, from what you wrote, that you have not been introduced at all by teachers so as to understand anything of the Hippocratic doctrines, and that you openly bring charges against things of which you have no knowledge at all; and you have been caught making a most ignorant refutation, attempting through it to overturn the constitution of every art, while, being ignorant of what Plato wrote about these matters, you often contradict yourself, corrupting the young, all those who, like you, being unexercised in logical theory, do not know how to distinguish true arguments from false.

lsj_entry_text: ἐξήγ-ησις, εως, ἡ, statement, narrative, ἐ. ποιήσασθαι Th. 1.72 ; ὑπέρ τινος Plb. 6.3.1 . explanation, interpretation, περὶ τοὺς νόμους Pl. Lg. 631a ; ἐνυπνίων D.S. 2.29 ; Ἐ. τῶν Ἐμπεδοκλέους, title of a work by Zeno Eleaticus; so in Gramm., Sch. Il. 8.296 .
greek_sentence: ἐφ’ ἅπασι δὲ τούτοις τολμηρότατός τε ἅμα καὶ φλύαρος ὤφθης, ἐπιχειρήσας γράφειν ἐξηγήσεις τῶν ὑφ’ Ἱπποκράτους εἰρημένων ἄνευ τοῦ μεμαθηκέναι πρότερον αὐτά.
english_sentence_A: On top of all this you have shown yourself at once most audacious and a babbler, having undertaken to write exegeses of what was said by Hippocrates without having first learned it.
english_sentence_B: On top of all this you were seen to be most audacious and at the same time a babbler, having undertaken to write exegeses of what was said by Hippocrates without first having learned it.
